title: In the Beginning
description: Read your first original Greek sentence and learn how cases reveal the structure of a sentence.
context: The Gospel of John opens with a deliberate reflection on the λόγος, the Word. The Greek is repetitive and structurally clear, making it useful for beginning readers.

grammar.title: The nominative
grammar.explanation: The nominative commonly marks the subject: the person or thing the sentence is about.

example.note: ὁ λόγος is nominative because λόγος is the subject.

grammar.title: The accusative
grammar.explanation: The accusative often marks the direct object, but it is also used after certain prepositions.

example.note: πρός takes the accusative here, so θεός appears as τὸν θεόν.

grammar.title: The dative
grammar.explanation: The dative can express location, means, possession and several other relationships.

example.note: ἐν normally takes the dative when describing location or position.

grammar.title: ἦν — he, she or it was
grammar.explanation: ἦν is an imperfect form of εἰμί, 'to be'. It means 'was' and is third-person singular.

texts.title: John 1:1
texts.greek: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
readingHints: Start by finding the repeated verb: ἦν.
Look for the nominative forms that tell you what each clause is about.
Notice that ἀρχή becomes ἀρχῇ after ἐν.
Notice that θεός becomes θεόν after πρός.
texts.translation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
